| **Farm Visit in PA-13**
---
| |
---
“My family put the herd together in 1928.”
---
As my eyes swept across the milking barn, Ayrshire, Jersey, and Holstein cows looked at me, chewed their cud, then put their heads through the bars to eat more feed.
---
I picked some up off the floor, smelled it, and rolled the moist mixture between my fingers. This wasn’t some kind of grain, but...woody.
---
“What’s this feed made of?” I asked the farmer, who had generously invited me to tour his dairy farm on this beautiful Thursday afternoon. This farm had originated in neighboring counties, then moved decades later to its current location in our 13th Congressional District where I am running for the office of U.S. Representative.
---
Forthright with his answers and always incredibly knowledgeable, he answered, “corn silage – fermented, hay/grass – fermented, ground corn (high moisture),” and the one that surprised me a little, “Purina pellets.” The exact combination was privileged information that came from a man I had briefly glimpsed earlier- the itinerant nutritionist – who obviously knew his stuff. Oh sure, this “suburbanite” (the farmer’s name for us nonfarm folks) had absolutely no real knowledge of a healthy cow, but once, years ago, I had correctly picked out which ones would win a blue ribbon at a State Fair. The bossies in front of me were clear-eyed, lowed harmoniously, and swished their tails in that casual, “there’s a fly around here somewheres” way that belied a contented lifestyle.
---
With 60-70 head of cattle on average, whose milk yields a butterfat content of 4.2%, well over the whole milk standard of 3.25%, this was the kind of farm straight out of the James Herriot book, “All Creatures Great and Small” that I had read voraciously as a child.
---
Did he name his cows, or were they just a number to him?
---
“Well, we got Blossom,” but then he added that his daughter had named some after the Princess Family.
---
“The Princess Family? What’s that?” I asked, ready to be charmed by some quaint royal lineage.
---
“Oh, you know, Ariel, Belle, and them.” I chuckled at the Disney reference.
---
But of course these cows had American names. We were in the heart of the Mid-Atlantic region, smack dab in the middle of South Central Pennsylvania. And where did his milk go? “Milk only flows East,” he explained. Some goes to Carlisle (charmingly pronounced “Car-lalle”) to turn into butter, however a good amount goes straight into some of the greatest Americana this country has ever known – Hershey’s chocolate.
---
I had been on the free Chocolate World ride at Hershey Park with my husband and children so many times, I could almost recite the script of production. At a critical point in the process, Hershey adds milk to the product. The script had always bragged the milk had been local and in a barn nestled among the hills of Appalachia, I was finding it truly was.
---
Unfortunately, this local farmer, like so many others, was suffering. When asked what the federal government could do for him, he was quick with his answer, “Milk pricing overhaul” and his wife who accompanied us on the tour, in addition to my campaign volunteer, Eileen Roberts, agreed wholeheartedly. Currently, the price runs $19/hundredweight. Hundredweight for us suburbanites is around 11.6 gallons.
---
A better price would be $28/hundredweight, like they had roughly “two years ago”, (when Biden was President, I thought quietly), but at least he added, “it’s not down to $14 like it was 3 years ago,” uh, also when Biden was President, I remembered.
---
Did the January passage of the federal “Whole Milk for Healthy Kids Act” help him?
---
Well, he hadn’t seen it yet, but he was sure it would help his bottom line. Caught between low milk prices, high fertilizer costs – about $23,000/month -, and high diesel prices that emblazoned every gas station marquee in startling numbers, the farmer has to keep balancing how much grain he’ll sell from his farmed over 150 acres of corn versus how much he’ll turn into silage that feeds his cows from those same fields. Even though he’s done it for years, and his only employees are his family, it’s a struggle to break even. According to Stoltzfus Grain website, Pennsylvania corn is trading at $5.10/bushel, but a better price according to the farmer would be $7/bushel. Specifically for corn, a bushel is 56 pounds. Sometimes, after paying his family, the farmer has no money left for himself or to upgrade his equipment. Maybe if there was some federal milk pricing, that might help, he hinted.
---
Would he sell his property to get out of this difficulty?
---
The farmer looked wistfully across his hillside farm and said it could get a person, “a satchel full of money, nothing else, a recipe to die,” and his wife nodded in agreement. I too nodded not knowing what to add, just sort of a politician’s yearning to do something for this fellow American whose job is to “feed America” as the Pennsylvania Farm Bureau so often reminds us. As yet, the Farm Bill hasn’t passed, so I could offer to vote to pass it, along with H.R. 9474 – Local Foods for Healthy Schools Act of 2026, when elected, but it just doesn’t seem immediate enough. Of course, I would vote to withdraw hostilities in Iran so the Strait of Hormuz could be opened, oil could be exported properly, and the prices of diesel and fertilizer would come down, but that is still months away.
---
We moved on to pet some baby goats who had come up to us, then we walked over to the manure pit – a concrete tub that stretched over 100 feet in diameter and had a depth of 10 feet. I peered through the chain link fence that surrounded it and looked at the brown muck. He pointed out the handy crust on top that kept the worst of the smells from putrefying the air and noted that it was about five feet high. “We give back to the ground” he said.
---
While the limit is 6000 gallons of manure an acre, the nitrogen from it doesn’t just infuse the ground. You have to have a “ground cover” he explained. Sweet clover was the original ground cover back in the 1970s, but legumes work pretty well too to convert the nitrogen in the manure into nitrogen in the soil.
---
All of a sudden, I thought back to my education in Maryland where all things led to the Chesapeake Bay. In my seventh grade year, I learned about the nitrogens coming off of the Pennsylvania farms, getting into the Bay, clouding up the water, preventing the bay grasses from growing which led to the worst possible outcome for any Marylander – a reduction of crabs to crack in the summer.
---
Was the farmer affected by those regulations at all?
---
“Too many regulations for the Chesapeake Bay,” he told me, and to make the point of overregulation, this registered Republican explained that the Army Corps of Engineers, in their infinite wisdom, had stretched the definition of “navigable water” to include his farmland.
---
“Does this look like navigable water to you?” he asked bluntly with a sweeping gesture of his arm. I could only shake my head vigorously. More importantly, he wasn’t losing dirt like had happened decades ago. In the 1970s his farm lost 30-40 tons of ground a year, now it was down to 3 tons, but the regulations didn’t recognize the improvement. This modern farmer doesn’t plow anymore – he uses sod. The Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS) measures how much his runoff is reduced and pays him based on his percentage through a cover crop program which requires planting multiple species by a deadline. Talking about those cover crops and runoff reminded him of something the federal government wasn’t getting right – he noted that the Federal Loan Rate hasn’t updated the base acreage of farms in years. So maybe, there was something more I could do for him.
---
After a jouncy ride through steeply-pitched fields that the farmer had acquired over the years and a brief hello a family member, who had been baling hay in a field, he reached the pinnacle of one field and turned the truck around. The view was utterly stunning. As the sun dazzled the valley spilling out below us, it was clear, the farmer doesn’t leave because there simply isn’t anywhere as beautiful.
---
(Note: the farmer is among many in the 13th Congressional District who are suffering the current administration’s follies, so he’s not named in order not to single him out.)
---
(Animal photo credit: Eileen Roberts)

| | **In Support of Recovery**
---
| |
---
On Tuesday, I was proud to walk with the Adams County Coalition for Overdose and Recovery in observance of International Overdose Awareness Day.
---
While I have never personally lost someone close to an overdose, the memorials hanging in the Sterner Building where the walk ended were a sober reminder of how prevalent addiction is and how much the community mourns the people lost to it.
---
Places like Mercy House in Gettysburg, part of TNH Sober Living, can exist because of federally funded programs like the Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinics.
---
As our elected U.S. Representative, I’ll do my utmost to strengthen funding to these and other Recovery programs so that we never add another picture to that memorial.
---
Together, we #ChooseDemocracy and Addiction Recovery!
---
| | |
---|---|---
---
| **SCRAP the CAP!**
---
| |
---
While there is a 3.6% Cost of Living Adjustment (COLA) for Social Security payments proposed to take place in early 2027, it is also true that Social Security payments are likely to be reduced by 22% in 2033.
---
The fix for that bleak future?
---
Scrap the Cap.
---
This means that high income earners should contribute based on all of their income, instead of only contributing from the first $184,500 of it.
---
In other words, the ultra-wealthy need to pay their fair share, just like the middle class are already doing.
---
If you agree that the Social Security fund should not be insolvent, please comment below.
---
And if you agree with the ultra-wealthy paying their fair share, write “Scrap the Cap” below.
---
If you have a different idea as to how to prevent Social Security insolvency, fell free to share that as well.
---
Please vote for me, Beth Farnham, on November 3rd so I can help vote this policy into Congress.
---

So, come to my Town Halls, ask me your important questions, listen to my answers, and then please vote for me on November 3rd, 2026. Together, we and REAL REPRESENTATION! | | | Farm Visit in PA-13 | | “My family put the herd together in 1928.” As my eyes swept across the milking barn, Ayrshire, Jersey, and Holstein cows looked at me, chewed their cud, then put their heads through the bars to eat more feed. I picked some up off the floor, smelled it, and rolled the moist mixture between my fingers. This wasn’t some kind of grain, but...woody. “What’s this feed made of?” I asked the farmer, who had generously invited me to tour his dairy farm on this beautiful Thursday afternoon. This farm had originated in neighboring counties, then moved decades later to its current location in our 13th Congressional District where I am running for the office of U.S. Representative. Forthright with his answers and always incredibly knowledgeable, he answered, “corn silage – fermented, hay/grass – fermented, ground corn (high moisture),” and the one that surprised me a little, “Purina pellets.” The exact combination was privileged information that came from a man I had briefly glimpsed earlier- the itinerant nutritionist – who obviously knew his stuff. Oh sure, this “suburbanite” (the farmer’s name for us nonfarm folks) had absolutely no real knowledge of a healthy cow, but once, years ago, I had correctly picked out which ones would win a blue ribbon at a State Fair. The bossies in front of me were clear-eyed, lowed harmoniously, and swished their tails in that casual, “there’s a fly around here somewheres” way that belied a contented lifestyle. With 60-70 head of cattle on average, whose milk yields a butterfat content of 4.2%, well over the whole milk standard of 3.25%, this was the kind of farm straight out of the James Herriot book, “All Creatures Great and Small” that I had read voraciously as a child. Did he name his cows, or were they just a number to him? “Well, we got Blossom,” but then he added that his daughter had named some after the Princess Family. “The Princess Family? What’s that?” I asked, ready to be charmed by some quaint royal lineage. “Oh, you know, Ariel, Belle, and them.” I chuckled at the Disney reference. But of course these cows had American names. We were in the heart of the Mid-Atlantic region, smack dab in the middle of South Central Pennsylvania. And where did his milk go? “Milk only flows East,” he explained. Some goes to Carlisle (charmingly pronounced “Car-lalle”) to turn into butter, however a good amount goes straight into some of the greatest Americana this country has ever known – Hershey’s chocolate. I had been on the free Chocolate World ride at Hershey Park with my husband and children so many times, I could almost recite the script of production. At a critical point in the process, Hershey adds milk to the product. The script had always bragged the milk had been local and in a barn nestled among the hills of Appalachia, I was finding it truly was. Unfortunately, this local farmer, like so many others, was suffering. When asked what the federal government could do for him, he was quick with his answer, “Milk pricing overhaul” and his wife who accompanied us on the tour, in addition to my campaign volunteer, Eileen Roberts, agreed wholeheartedly. Currently, the price runs $19/hundredweight. Hundredweight for us suburbanites is around 11.6 gallons. A better price would be $28/hundredweight, like they had roughly “two years ago”, (when Biden was President, I thought quietly), but at least he added, “it’s not down to $14 like it was 3 years ago,” uh, also when Biden was President, I remembered. Did the January passage of the federal “Whole Milk for Healthy Kids Act” help him? Well, he hadn’t seen it yet, but he was sure it would help his bottom line. Caught between low milk prices, high fertilizer costs – about $23,000/month -, and high diesel prices that emblazoned every gas station marquee in startling numbers, the farmer has to keep balancing how much grain he’ll sell from his farmed over 150 acres of corn versus how much he’ll turn into silage that feeds his cows from those same fields. Even though he’s done it for years, and his only employees are his family, it’s a struggle to break even. According to Stoltzfus Grain website, Pennsylvania corn is trading at $5.10/bushel, but a better price according to the farmer would be $7/bushel. Specifically for corn, a bushel is 56 pounds. Sometimes, after paying his family, the farmer has no money left for himself or to upgrade his equipment. Maybe if there was some federal milk pricing, that might help, he hinted. Would he sell his property to get out of this difficulty? The farmer looked wistfully across his hillside farm and said it could get a person, “a satchel full of money, nothing else, a recipe to die,” and his wife nodded in agreement. I too nodded not knowing what to add, just sort of a politician’s yearning to do something for this fellow American whose job is to “feed America” as the Pennsylvania Farm Bureau so often reminds us. As yet, the Farm Bill hasn’t passed, so I could offer to vote to pass it, along with H.R. 9474 – Local Foods for Healthy Schools Act of 2026, when elected, but it just doesn’t seem immediate enough. Of course, I would vote to withdraw hostilities in Iran so the Strait of Hormuz could be opened, oil could be exported properly, and the prices of diesel and fertilizer would come down, but that is still months away. We moved on to pet some baby goats who had come up to us, then we walked over to the manure pit – a concrete tub that stretched over 100 feet in diameter and had a depth of 10 feet. I peered through the chain link fence that surrounded it and looked at the brown muck. He pointed out the handy crust on top that kept the worst of the smells from putrefying the air and noted that it was about five feet high. “We give back to the ground” he said. While the limit is 6000 gallons of manure an acre, the nitrogen from it doesn’t just infuse the ground. You have to have a “ground cover” he explained. Sweet clover was the original ground cover back in the 1970s, but legumes work pretty well too to convert the nitrogen in the manure into nitrogen in the soil. All of a sudden, I thought back to my education in Maryland where all things led to the Chesapeake Bay. In my seventh grade year, I learned about the nitrogens coming off of the Pennsylvania farms, getting into the Bay, clouding up the water, preventing the bay grasses from growing which led to the worst possible outcome for any Marylander – a reduction of crabs to crack in the summer. Was the farmer affected by those regulations at all? “Too many regulations for the Chesapeake Bay,” he told me, and to make the point of overregulation, this registered Republican explained that the Army Corps of Engineers, in their infinite wisdom, had stretched the definition of “navigable water” to include his farmland. “Does this look like navigable water to you?” he asked bluntly with a sweeping gesture of his arm. I could only shake my head vigorously. More importantly, he wasn’t losing dirt like had happened decades ago. In the 1970s his farm lost 30-40 tons of ground a year, now it was down to 3 tons, but the regulations didn’t recognize the improvement. This modern farmer doesn’t plow anymore – he uses sod. The Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS) measures how much his runoff is reduced and pays him based on his percentage through a cover crop program which requires planting multiple species by a deadline. Talking about those cover crops and runoff reminded him of something the federal government wasn’t getting right – he noted that the Federal Loan Rate hasn’t updated the base acreage of farms in years. So maybe, there was something more I could do for him. After a jouncy ride through steeply-pitched fields that the farmer had acquired over the years and a brief hello a family member, who had been baling hay in a field, he reached the pinnacle of one field and turned the truck around. The view was utterly stunning. As the sun dazzled the valley spilling out below us, it was clear, the farmer doesn’t leave because there simply isn’t anywhere as beautiful. (Note: the farmer is among many in the 13th Congressional District who are suffering the current administration’s follies, so he’s not named in order not to single him out.) (Animal photo credit: Eileen Roberts) | | ---|--- | | In Support of Recovery | | On Tuesday, I was proud to walk with the Adams County Coalition for Overdose and Recovery in observance of International Overdose Awareness Day. While I have never personally lost someone close to an overdose, the memorials hanging in the Sterner Building where the walk ended were a sober reminder of how prevalent addiction is and how much the community mourns the people lost to it. Places like Mercy House in Gettysburg, part of TNH Sober Living, can exist because of federally funded programs like the Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinics. As our elected U.S. Representative, I’ll do my utmost to strengthen funding to these and other Recovery programs so that we never add another picture to that memorial. Please vote for me, Beth Farnham, on November 3rd so I can help vote this policy into Congress. Together, we #ChooseDemocracy and aging with dignity! I promised South Carolina I'd carry the conservative agenda to the Senate for six more years. President Trump stood with me and told you why he trusts me, too. I'm not letting her bank account break that promise. The general is November 3 - less than 65 days out. Every week from now until then, she's on TV, in your mailbox, on your phone. We can't answer that with an empty account. I need you in the next 48 hours. Don't let the most radical candidate South Carolina Democrats have ever nominated buy this seat. body:
Hey there,
I'll keep this short. We missed our goal last month, and we've been playing catch up ever since.
I don't love asking for your support more than I have to, but I'd be lying if I said I wasn't worried.
If you can spare $5 or anything today, it would _really_ help us in the long run:
**[https://secure.actblue.com/donate/em_ms_af_20260906_2_ak](https://act.fordfornevada.com/go/86?c0=em_ms_af_20260906_2_ak.TS3td4&refcode=em20260906-828&t=2&akid=828%2E127862%2E1EEIrB)**
We recently launched a new TV ad about the disastrous impact the Lombardo-Trump economy has had on Nevada families, and how our campaign’s agenda is focused on delivering much-needed relief by lowering housing costs, making health care affordable, and delivering clean, affordable energy across the state.

Peter, I
want to tell you about a man named Mr. Larry:

[ Mr. ]Mr. Larry

On his way to work one day, he was in a car accident.

Despite having health insurance, Mr. Larry ended up with thousands of
dollars in medical debt. All because of one accident.

This series of events is far too common in America. One trip to the doctor
or hospital can quickly spiral into years of financial burden.

Meanwhile, insurance CEOs rake in record profits year after year. It’s
completely unfair.

But Mr. Larry’s story didn’t end there. One day, he got a letter in the
mail saying his debt was cleaned.

That letter came from a program I fought for as director of Wayne County’s
Department of Health, Human and Veterans’ Services, which is set to cancel
$700 million in medical debt for 300,000 Michiganders. Mr. Larry was one
of those Michiganders.

We met up with Mr. Larry and told this story in an ad we released this
summer:

[ A ]A thumbnail of the ad featuring Abdul and Mr. Larry

--------------------------------------------------------------------------

Peter, that's
what a doctor with a little bit of power can do from a local-level
position.

Just imagine what we can accomplish in the U.S. Senate.

This is the type of progress I’m fighting for, because in the richest,
most powerful country in the world, getting the care you need shouldn’t
come at the expense of a lifetime of debt.

That’s why I’m fighting to pass Medicare for All and abolish medical debt
for every American. And I’m not afraid to take on Big Pharma or any
corporate interest that stands in the way of us making that progress real.

But I can’t do this alone. The groups that profit off medical debt do not
want a doctor in the U.S. Senate.

They want their errand boy, MAGA Mike Rogers, in the Senate to make them
richer.

Peter, I need
your help to defeat Mike Rogers and the $51 million he’s got to boost his
campaign over the airwaves.

| Hi Friend — There is a lot of noise around elections right now. So many headlines, they can give a person whiplash. But one of the most powerful things we can do is remarkably simple: Check your own voter record. Go to [ScanCheckProtect.org](https://de717de0.click.kit-mail3.com/xmu9er6g3ph6hp4mevqc5h20r2gwlsnh28k4m/z2hghnhel6vogouph0/aHR0cHM6Ly9zY2FuY2hlY2twcm90ZWN0Lm9yZw==) and confirm that your registration and voting history is accurate. Check the other voters in your household. And if you’ve moved, check your previous addresses to make sure an old registration isn’t still active. | [](https://de717de0.click.kit-mail3.com/xmu9er6g3ph6hp4mevqc5h20r2gwlsnh28k4m/z2hghnhel6vogouph0/aHR0cHM6Ly9zY2FuY2hlY2twcm90ZWN0Lm9yZw==)[https://scancheckprotect.org](https://de717de0.click.kit-mail3.com/xmu9er6g3ph6hp4mevqc5h20r2gwlsnh28k4m/z2hghnhel6vogouph0/aHR0cHM6Ly9zY2FuY2hlY2twcm90ZWN0Lm9yZw==)
---
If something doesn’t look right, [Scan. Check. Protect.](https://de717de0.click.kit-mail3.com/xmu9er6g3ph6hp4mevqc5h20r2gwlsnh28k4m/z2hghnhel6vogouph0/aHR0cHM6Ly9zY2FuY2hlY2twcm90ZWN0Lm9yZw==) equips you to report it right then and there.
You can follow the prompts, document what you found, and take the appropriate next steps. You don’t have to wonder what to do or where to start.
---
Scan. Check. Protect.
It takes only a few minutes. Then send it to your family and friends and ask them to do the same.
Imagine what happens when millions of Americans take responsibility for confirming their own records.
This is how we strengthen election integrity — citizen by citizen, household by household.
Keep the faith. Never quit. Ephesians 6 FTW!
Ever onward —
---

Alright, Derek – let’s walk through this together:
Growing up, my family faced challenges that many Wisconsinites know all too well, including addiction, mental health challenges, and unstable housing. I never knew if I would come home to find our belongings on the curb from another eviction, food in the refrigerator, or a safe place to land. My parents worked hard, but it was tough.
**Luckily, I had people in my community who believed in me and gave me opportunities that changed my life.**
They helped me graduate from high school, supported my passion for public service, and helped me run for elected office. They also helped me return to college to finish my undergraduate degree while serving as Milwaukee County executive.
I’ve had an unconventional path, Derek, but my community has had my back every step of the way. **I believe every person, every family deserves that same support.**
That belief shaped my priorities as Milwaukee County executive, and it’s why I’m running for governor now. I’ve seen first-hand what happens when we put working families first:
→ When we expanded access to affordable housing, **our per capita unhoused population dropped to _the lowest in the nation_**. Now, fewer families suffer the upheaval of eviction that my family faced.
→ When we expanded healthcare access – including opening a 24/7 walk-in mental health emergency center – **our community felt the relief of _safe, comprehensive care close to home_**. That’s a resource I wish my parents would've had.
→ When we invested in public transit and local parks, **our communities thrived with new opportunities to stay connected and active.** Now, folks from backgrounds like mine have greater access to the kinds of opportunities that helped me thrive.
**But, Derek, this is just the beginning.**
I’m serious about fighting to make life better for working families across Wisconsin. I’m serious about lowering costs, funding our public schools, expanding access to healthcare and public services. I’m serious about building a Wisconsin where working people can build a life they love without leaving the state they love.
**So, Derek, my cards are on the table. You’ve seen my track record, and you’ve heard my vision for the future of Wisconsin. clean_body: I’m laying all my cards on the table so you can see my track record for yourself. | | | | During the next 58 days of this campaign, you’ll hear me talk a lot about how my working-class background shapes my vision for Wisconsin’s future. That’s not just a talking point, Derek. It’s how I govern. But I won’t ask you to take my word for it. Today, I want to lay all my cards on the table so you can see my track record for yourself. This is a longer email than I usually send, and I really hope you’ll stick around to hear my story. | | Alright, Derek – let’s walk through this together: Growing up, my family faced challenges that many Wisconsinites know all too well, including addiction, mental health challenges, and unstable housing. I never knew if I would come home to find our belongings on the curb from another eviction, food in the refrigerator, or a safe place to land. My parents worked hard, but it was tough. Luckily, I had people in my community who believed in me and gave me opportunities that changed my life. They helped me graduate from high school, supported my passion for public service, and helped me run for elected office. They also helped me return to college to finish my undergraduate degree while serving as Milwaukee County executive. I’ve had an unconventional path, Derek, but my community has had my back every step of the way. I believe every person, every family deserves that same support. That belief shaped my priorities as Milwaukee County executive, and it’s why I’m running for governor now. I’ve seen first-hand what happens when we put working families first: → When we expanded access to affordable housing, our per capita unhoused population dropped to the lowest in the nation. Now, fewer families suffer the upheaval of eviction that my family faced. → When we expanded healthcare access – including opening a 24/7 walk-in mental health emergency center – our community felt the relief of safe, comprehensive care close to home. That’s a resource I wish my parents would've had. → When we invested in public transit and local parks, our communities thrived with new opportunities to stay connected and active. Now, folks from backgrounds like mine have greater access to the kinds of opportunities that helped me thrive. But, Derek, this is just the beginning. I’m serious about fighting to make life better for working families across Wisconsin. I’m serious about lowering costs, funding our public schools, expanding access to healthcare and public services. I’m serious about building a Wisconsin where working people can build a life they love without leaving the state they love. So, Derek, my cards are on the table. You’ve seen my track record, and you’ve heard my vision for the future of Wisconsin. Now, I’m asking you to stand with me to make it a reality. while I certainly don’t expect you or anyone else to donate to every email my team and I send, I hope you’ll consider donating to this one.
# [](https://act.electjon.com/go/4629?t=1&akid=2816%2E5691347%2EF1r-JV)

Peter,
Let me guess: when you open up your email inbox, you’re bombarded with emails from political campaigns or advocacy organizations, some of which you may not have even heard of.
I know it’s a lot. And it’s why in a sea of promises that “Donald Trump is FINISHED” and breathless “5X MATCH NOW!!!” emails, I work really hard to make sure our messages are different.

name: Gavin Newsom
subject: Something HUGE happening in rural and red America right now
disclaimer_text: PAID FOR BY CAMPAIGN FOR DEMOCRACY PAC
body:
I just wrapped up my trip to Alabama, South Carolina and North Carolina and let me say that energy is undeniable.

There is something HUGE happening in rural and red America right now. I just wrapped up my trip to Alabama, South Carolina and North Carolina and people are PISSED at what Donald Trump has done to our country.
The energy is undeniable. Many of these southern states are far too often neglected by our party, but what I saw is people in communities showing up for themselves and for each other. They are fired up and they are getting organized to support campaigns at the top of the ticket and for down ballot elections.
In a moment, I am going to ask you to help those state parties. Because if they have the resources to FIGHT, they are going to win a lot of races this November and stop Trump’s MAGA agenda.
And if we can win in the South, Donald Trump's presidency will be over as we know it.
Look at this: An absolutely packed house in rural South Carolina.
[](https://secure.actblue.com/donate/ggn-nc-sc-al?refcode=ggn-em260906&refcode2=3020_4767699_A3OWf5&akid=3020%2E4767699%2EA3OWf5)
We held several events in the state -- each attended by more people than the last. Hundreds showed up to volunteer their time and their efforts to elect Democrats in the state.
[](https://secure.actblue.com/donate/ggn-nc-sc-al?refcode=ggn-em260906&refcode2=3020_4767699_A3OWf5&akid=3020%2E4767699%2EA3OWf5)
Same thing in North Carolina. Here's a photo at a canvass kick-off for Roy Cooper and other Democrats up and down the ballot.
[](https://secure.actblue.com/donate/ggn-nc-sc-al?refcode=ggn-em260906&refcode2=3020_4767699_A3OWf5&akid=3020%2E4767699%2EA3OWf5)
And we closed it all out with a large rally with the North Carolina Democratic Party.
But like I've mentioned before: a lot of these states in the South are long-neglected financially. All the so-called "Swing States" and the top Senate races in the country attract the big bucks from small-dollar and super PACs.
This happens all while Democratic parties in South Carolina and Alabama struggle financially -- even while the people in these states volunteer just as much (or more) than anywhere else in the country.
That's why I am reaching out to ask you to support some of those states today. Because if you do, then Democrats truly can and will win everywhere this November.
